analysis.one_liner: Taxed oil companies' windfall profits and directed the money to home energy help for low-income families.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2005 with no cosponsors, the bill sat in three House committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 50% excise tax on the profits integrated oil companies make from selling crude above an inflation-adjusted $40-per-barrel baseline. It would last three years, exempt newly discovered oil, and credit money the companies invest in drilling, refineries, and fuel facilities. All the revenue raised would go to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills. The bill was referred to three House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that receive LIHEAP help paying energy bills, at a time — right after the 2005 hurricane season — when oil and home heating prices had spiked.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households facing high energy bills

how_it_helps.text: All windfall-tax revenue would be appropriated solely to carry out LIHEAP, the federal program that helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills [S3].
The tax applies only to profits above a $40-per-barrel baseline adjusted for inflation, so it targets the excess profits earned when oil prices spike rather than ordinary returns [S2, S3].

The bill credits companies' investments in drilling, refinery property, renewable fuel facilities, and ethanol or biodiesel production against the tax, directing oil-industry capital toward new supply rather than simply confiscating it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies, which would pay half of their windfall profit from crude production each year for three years, with the tax deductible against income taxes [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax is deductible against income taxes and sunsets after three years, and it excludes oil from newly drilled wells, all of which narrow how much revenue it would actually raise for LIHEAP [S3].

Critics of windfall profits taxes argue they discourage domestic oil production and can be passed through to consumers as higher prices; this bill tries to blunt that by exempting new wells and crediting investment, but the exemption also shrinks the tax base [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design tries to thread the needle: it taxes only profits above an inflation-adjusted $40 baseline, shields new drilling, credits investment, and sunsets after three years. Those guardrails also cut the revenue available for LIHEAP, and the deductibility further reduces the take. Still, the core trade is straightforward — a slice of oil-company windfall during a price spike funds energy help for poor households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and to two subcommittees, got zero cosponsors, and died when the 109th Congress ended without any committee or floor vote [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on November 8, 2005, shortly after oil and gasoline prices spiked in the wake of the 2005 hurricanes [S1, S2].

It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce committees, and later to the Energy and Air Quality and Education Reform subcommittees, but no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed [S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill, and it never advanced before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies kept their windfall profits untaxed, and LIHEAP received none of the revenue this bill would have directed to it.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; controlled any markup of the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and committee chairs of the Republican-controlled House
against.what_they_did: Let the bill sit in committee for the rest of the Congress without scheduling action.

sides.party_line_note: A lone House Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republicans or other Democrats signed on as cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled House never acted on it [S4, S1].

industries.note: They would pay a 50% excise tax on profits from crude sold above an inflation-adjusted $40 baseline for three years. Their interest in defeating the bill ran against low-income households seeking help with heating bills driven up by the same price spike.

industries.industry: LIHEAP recipient households and the home-energy assistance sector
industries.note: The bill would have appropriated every dollar of the new tax to LIHEAP, expanding help for low-income energy bills. It never received funding because the bill died.
